title: runtime-benchmarking-harness-perf-regression-notes-v2
content:
Purpose:
This working doc captures the current state of the runtime benchmarking harness, microbench suites, and perf-regression notes focused on kernels, scheduler behavior, and KV cache effects. Goal is to have reproducible microbenchmarks + trace artifacts we can use in CI (perf-regression checks) and in incident RCA.

Scope:
- Kernel microbenchmarks: attention, matmul, softmax, rotary/fused kernels, quantized kernels (int8/4-bit)
- Scheduling tests: dynamic batching, preemption, multi-tenant fairness, latency SLO enforcement
- KV cache: prefix reuse patterns, hit/miss amplification, eviction policies, memory accounting
- Traces: end-to-end request traces (flame graphs, CPU/GPU timelines), RPC latency breakdowns

Summary of current harness (high-level):
- harness repo: serving-runtime/tools/bench (see linked PR)
- runner types: local (single host), cluster (k8s job), synthetic-client (in-process load generator), real-client (grpc/HTTP loadgen client)
- measurement outputs: JSON per run (latency histogram, token throughput, kernel counters), optional trace.zip with perf events and GPU CUPTI traces
- baselines: nightly baselines stored under s3://redwood-perf/baselines/{date}/{model}/{config}.json

How to run (quick):
- Docker quick run for microbench:
  ./bench/local_run.sh --model gpt2-small --suite kernel --kernel attention --seq 512 --threads 8 --iters 200
- Cluster: k8s job template serving-runtime/bench/job.yaml; edit env for MODEL, SUITE, SEED
- CI integration (prototype): .github/workflows/perf.yml triggers harness on linux-gpu runners for changed PR files under serving-runtime/src/*.cu or src/scheduler/*

Microbench suites (examples):
1) Kernels/single-op
- attention-forward/backward: vary seq_len {64,128,256,512,1024}, batch {1,2,4}, heads {12,16}, dtype {fp16, int8}
- matmul-large: test shapes representative of FFN and KV projections
- softmax-stability: stress test over long sequences to catch numerical regressions and divergence
- fused-rotary + qkv-fusion: measuring combined kernel performance vs non-fused baseline

2) KV cache microbench
- prefix-reuse patterns: run workloads with prefix lengths {0,32,128,512} and measure incremental token RT/throughput
- hit-rate injection: synthetic workload to set cache hit rate to {0%,25%,50%,75%,90%} to see latency tail amplification
- eviction stress test: simulate memory pressure and validate that eviction policy (LRU vs segmented LRU) respects invariants and that request latency recovers

3) Scheduler/batching tests
- dynamic batching latency SLO tests: schedule mixed request sizes and assert p99 latency < configured SLO when under provisioned/over provisioned
- preemption fairness: high-priority requests should not see >2x latency multiplier vs baseline
- multi-tenant isolation: two tenants A/B with different concurrency; verify throughput fairness and lack of noisy neighbor amplification

Typical metrics we collect per run:
- p50/p90/p99 latency (ms) for token generation and for first-token
- tokens/sec (aggregate) and tokens/sec per GPU
- kernel utilization % (GPU SM occupancy), kernel time breakdown (ms)
- CPU thread blocked time, context switches, memcpy times
- KV cache hit rate, average KV fetch time, memory usage (RSS + GPU memory)
- scheduling counters: batch sizes distribution, queue wait times, preemption counts

Perf regression detection strategy:
- nightly baselines + windowed comparisons (7-day median baseline)
- threshold rules: regressions flagged if p99 latency increases >15% AND tokens/sec decreases >10% OR kernel time increase >20% on critical kernels
- automated artifact collection on PR: run a 5-min microbench (subset) and upload JSON + traces and compare to target baseline; if flagged, block merge and post annotations to PR
- human-in-loop: require eng-serving-runtime reviewer to triage automated flags and attach root-cause note

Recent runs and notable regressions (notes):
- 2024-09-20: spike in p99 for seq=512, int8 attention forward after merging fused-kernel rewrite (PR #402). Investigation: increased register pressure leading to lower occupancy. Action: revert patch and iterate on tiling strategy. (JIRA INF-2345 opened)
- 2024-09-27: KV cache miss amplification seen with prefix reuse when batch coalescing enabled. Observed increased latency tail due to stale cache pointer reuse across batches. Patch: enforce cache object ownership per request and add per-batch cache validation. (see PR 411)

Trace artifacts (examples and how we store them):
- trace files zipped into s3://redwood-perf/traces/{run_id}.zip. Each zip contains:
  - bench-output.json (latency hist, kernel counters)
  - flamegraph.svg (CPU-side stack sampling during run)
  - cuptrace.nv (CUPTI capture) or nsight timelines for GPU runs
  - perf-record.data (Linux perf)
- example quick analysis: open flamegraph.svg and inspect 'scheduler::acquire_batch' stack height to measure queue wait proportion.

Investigation checklist for new regression:
- reproduce locally with identical harness args and pinned docker image
- collect perf counters: nvprof/CUPTI, nsys, perf top, and CPU flamegraph
- instrument scheduling debug counters (enable SCHED_DEBUG env -> emits per-request traces)
- compare kernel-level traces vs baseline (kernel time deltas)

Open design/engineering questions (todo):
- Should CI run both fp16 and int8 microbench subsets on every PR touching kernels? Cost tradeoff vs speed. Proposal: run fp16 subset on PR, int8 nightly and on PRs that modify quantization/kernels.
- How best to tag baseline runs for model architecture variants? We currently use model name + quantization string but need to include 'kernel-variant' to avoid false positives when testing compiler-generated kernels.
- Can we adopt bpftrace to get lower-overhead stack traces for production-like latency tail investigation?

Short-term action items (owners):
- Asha: wire PR annotation bot to post harness summary & link to trace (due 2024-10-10)
- Miguel: add int8 microbench subset to nightly runs and add baseline uploader job (due 2024-10-03)
- Samira: prototype bpftrace capture on staging to evaluate overhead (due 2024-10-17)
- Ethan: add scheduler debug env var that emits per-request JSON trace for first 100 requests in a run (due 2024-10-07)

Notes on noise and flakiness (lessons learned):
- GPU thermal throttling introduces noisiness during long runs; nightly baselines run with 'cooldown' windows and GPU frequency pinned where possible
- Container startup jitter: use pre-warmed node pools for baselines to reduce cold-start variance
- Network variability: when comparing across regions, ensure cross-region latency is excluded or measured separately

Appendix: useful commands and snippets
- run local kernel microbench (example):
  ./bench/bin/kernel_microbench --kernel attention --seq 512 --dtype int8 --gpu 0 --iters 500 --warmup 50 --out /tmp/run123
- collect CUPTI timeline (nsys):
  nsys profile -o /tmp/trace --trace=cuda,osrt ./bench/bin/run_workload --config configs/seq512.json
- baseline diff tool (proto):
  python tools/baseline_diff.py --baseline s3://redwood-perf/baselines/2024-08-01/gpt2-small-int8.json --run /tmp/run123/bench-output.json --rules rules/regression_rules.yaml

Work-in-progress items (WIP):
- auto-triage rules that map kernel regressions to likely causes (tiling, register pressure, memory copies) based on counter signatures
- add metric-normalization to account for different GPU generations (e.g., normalize by theoretical TFLOPS or SM count)

References and related artifacts:
- GitHub PRs: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/402, /pull/411
- JIRA: INF-2345 (attention kernel regression), INF-2390 (kv-cache eviction bug)
- Confluence: Runtime Benchmarking best practices (linked above)

End of notes. This is a living document; expect edits as we stabilize the CI and triage flows.
